claim: Humans, monkeys, rats and mice all follow the marginal value theorem qualitatively: they stay longer (leave at a lower reward threshold) when travel is longer or the environment is poorer, and leave at a higher threshold in richer environments; they also stay longer in richer patches.
agent_test: Give the agent a switching cost at 3 levels; check that the stay length (steps before switching operator) rises with cost, on a matched token budget.
audit_note: Under MVT a richer environment lowers stay time (higher leaving threshold); sources show thresholds fall in poorer environments (longer travel, steeper depletion), so 'stay longer when the environment is richer' is reversed; richness only raises stays at the patch level.
claim_before_audit: Humans, monkeys, rats and mice all follow the marginal value theorem qualitatively: they stay longer in a patch when travel is longer or the environment is richer, and leave earlier when depletion is steep.

claim: Almost every tested forager overharvests: it leaves later than the average-rate rule says (monkeys +2.2 s, humans 9-10 percent below optimal earnings, rats +3.4 trials).
agent_test: Measure the agent's overstay against the rule at equal tokens; test whether a trigger set slightly below the average rate beats exact equality.
audit_note: Overharvesting is not universal in the cited sources (no overharvesting on rich planets in Harhen, gerbils did not overstay in Guldener, early leaving in some Wolfe conditions); the 'almost every' hedge covers this; the human figure is an earnings loss of about 10 percent, not a stay-time measure.

claim: A learning-and-uncertainty account (rich-poor mix, uncertainty-adaptive discounting) explains much of human overharvesting in one task (Harhen and Bornstein 2023): it shrank with experience and was absent in rich environments; but a residual overharvesting bias remains in other human work (Constantino and Daw 2015) and rats overharvested in every condition (Kane 2019).
agent_test: Give the agent a table of earlier yields; check whether overstay shrinks versus a cold start.
audit_note: Harhen and Bornstein explain overharvesting with their own model in one human task; Constantino and Daw still find a significant residual overharvesting bias in the MVT learning model, and Kane's rats overharvested in every condition.
claim_before_audit: Overharvesting is largely explained by learning and uncertainty (rich-poor mix, discounting), not a fixed bias: it shrinks with experience and is absent in rich environments.

claim: Patch leaving is better described as inference about patch quality (Bayesian updating) than a plain rate comparison, but the winning rule depends on the setting (baboons: Bayesian in the experiment, MVT in the wild; mice: Bayesian best at high stochasticity).
agent_test: Compare three triggers at equal tokens: constant step count, running-average-rate, and a belief-based trigger that updates a yield estimate.

claim: Simple heuristics (constant time, count of rewards) do about as well as MVT when stochasticity is low (RMSE 4.88 vs 4.90 in mice).
agent_test: Include a fixed budget-per-operator baseline in every comparison; expect it to be hard to beat on easy items.

claim: The Kolling 2012 claim that dACC tracks the value of foraging (search) is challenged: dACC activity followed choice difficulty when the two were decoupled (Shenhav 2014), and Kolling 2016 replied that shared variance was below 2.5 percent in their design.
agent_test: None directly. Do not rely on the neural claim; the behavioural rule stands on animal and human behaviour data.

claim: Humans show a bias against searching or switching: they need more objective gain to forage than to engage (indifference point at foraging value 1.65 and 5.0 in two Shenhav samples).
agent_test: Check whether the agent keeps an operator longer than a value-equal alternative would justify; measure the yield gap needed before it switches.
audit_note: Both indifference points come from Experiments 1 and 2 of one paper (Shenhav 2014); Kolling 2012 gives the bias qualitatively.

claim: Stress, dopamine state, apathy and childhood adversity shift patch-leaving thresholds in humans (higher cortisol response: lower exit threshold, i.e. staying longer).
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM; treat as evidence that the threshold is a tunable parameter, not a fixed one.

claim: Leaving times vary between trials even in identical contexts, and this variability is better explained by stochastic choice than by learning noise.
agent_test: Run the same item several times; check whether the switch step varies. If so, consider a stochastic trigger or a vote across runs.

claim: Free-running LLMs switch categories less than humans in semantic fluency (switch ratio 0.40 vs 0.55 in Llama-3), so they stay in a patch longer, but their transition structure matches humans (Spearman 0.701).
agent_test: Count how often the agent abandons an exhausted line of attack without a prompt; compare with a prompt that states the current yield.

claim: Inside open LLMs, the chance of leaving a category rises as the unsaid in-category items among the strongest internal concepts run out (r at least 0.31, five models, 2B-9B), and a steering vector moves the switch rate from 0.29 to 0.70 or 0.07 in Gemma-2-9B.
agent_test: Needs white-box access; a black-box proxy is the count of fresh versus repeated items in the last outputs.

claim: A switch probe on natural human data is near chance (AUROC 0.57), so the high AUROCs depend on exaggerated contrast sets.
agent_test: Do not build on activation probes for switch detection without testing on natural data.

claim: Deep RL agents learn near-MVT leaving: recurrent agents overstay the plain MVT optimum by 15.8 steps but match discounted MVT (+0.9 steps, p=0.74), and the world-model agent (DreamerV2) lands near the optimum while model-free PPO does not.
agent_test: For a scaffold, set the threshold slightly more patient than the plain rule; train nothing.
audit_note: 'Match discounted MVT' means not significantly different (p=0.74, n=12 agents); Fonseca is a preprint with three training runs per algorithm.

claim: Raw-history LLMs fail to explore in bandits (GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure in more than 60 percent of replicates); the fix is to hand the model summary statistics, and code interpreters and reasoning mode help in later work. Handing the numbers over only partly closes the gap: Gemini-1.5 Pro overall win rate 45.5 (raw) to 60.0 (summary) to 59.6 (algorithm-guided) against 90.6 for UCB; Gemma 2B and 9B did not gain.
agent_test: Let code or a counter compute yield per operator and feed the number to the model; compare with the model estimating yield from the raw transcript, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Gemma-2B did gain slightly with summarised history (7.6 to 10.5) but fell with algorithm guidance (4.9); Gemma-9B fell (10.5 to 5.3 and 4.1).

claim: No study found tests a depleting-patch leave rule (Kolling or Constantino-Daw style task) on an LLM, and none uses 'yield below running average' as a stop trigger; working systems use fixed timers, step discounts or sufficiency checks. A second search pass (gap search) again found none; closest are confidence-based early exits (DEER, probe exit, answer consistency), which are level rules, not rate rules.
agent_test: This is open ground: run the agent through the patch paradigm and vary the leave rule.

claim: Efficiency penalties on steps help retrieval agents (InForage) and sufficiency-based stopping saves tokens (SCOUT 29.7k vs 273.9k for Gemini-3-Pro at a higher score), but leaving too early is costly (a knowledge cliff below 15,000 characters of context; one-author, weak).
agent_test: Sweep the stop point (early, average-rate, late) at equal tokens and plot accuracy; look for the cliff.

claim: Overthinking in reasoning models is a stopping failure: later solution rounds add little (first round correct in over 92% of correct cases and under 60% of tokens), and shortening or early exit kept accuracy (24% fewer tokens at equal accuracy with a probe exit; 19.1-80.1% shorter chains with DEER). Forced extra thinking eventually lowers accuracy (87.3% to 70.3%).
agent_test: Use a per-problem yield check (new information per step) to cut steps on easy items; verify accuracy holds. Compare against a fixed-step stop and a sufficiency stop at equal tokens.
audit_note: Chen et al. say 'in more than 92% of cases' the first round is correct; the 60% token share is 'generally less than 60%'; the 87.3 to 70.3 decline is one model/benchmark setting in Ghosal et al.

claim: Semantic fluency in people moves between clusters when the within-cluster retrieval rate falls below the global average (Hills 2012), but a random-walk account competes and an LLM-generator comparison did not settle it; random walks on modern embeddings give MVT-like foraging while Metropolis-Hastings does not.
agent_test: None needed beyond noting that the rule may emerge from simple retrieval dynamics.

claim: The leave rule assumes a known, deterministic depletion curve; when this is unknown, the best rule changes with patch variability (about a 25 percent threshold between counting and timing rules).
agent_test: Vary how noisy the yield signal is; check which trigger wins at each noise level.

claim: Adaptive confidence-based exit beats a fixed-step exit at equal token cost in one test (87.4% vs about 82.5% accuracy at similar tokens, R1-Distill-Llama-8B on MATH). No test uses a yield-below-average trigger.
agent_test: Run three arms at equal tokens: fixed-step, sufficiency check, yield-below-average. Report accuracy per token.

claim: The yield curve of extra thinking has a peak: accuracy rises then falls with forced extra thinking (82.2 to 87.3 to 70.3 percent), flattens near six forced continuations (s1), and repeated sampling gives log-linear coverage (15.9% to 56% from 1 to 250 samples). So a finite optimal leave point exists, and restarting beats staying late.
agent_test: Estimate the marginal gain per step for each operator on a pilot set; set the threshold from it.
audit_note: Peak result is from one model and setting in Ghosal et al. (which also says there is no reliable stopping criterion); the repeated-sampling figure is coverage with an oracle verifier, not accuracy.

claim: Underthinking is the mirror error: on hard items o1-like models switch thoughts too often (418% more switches in wrong answers, 225% more tokens), and a decoding penalty on switching raised accuracy (DeepSeek-R1 on AIME2024 switch tokens 13.8 to 5.7). A single leave rule tuned on easy items can worsen hard items.
agent_test: Report stop behaviour split by item difficulty; add a floor on dwell time before a leave is allowed.

claim: Optimal leave time under discounting is longer than the plain MVT time when yield only falls, and shorter when later payoffs can rise (Zylberberg 2024, theory). The best threshold is therefore not fixed at the average rate, and no LLM calibration of the margin exists.
agent_test: Test thresholds at 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 times the running average; check the margin on noisy and on insight-style items.

claim: Longer travel (switch) cost lengthens stays in learning agents (Wispinski: patch distance 5-12 m), and raising the cost of switching thoughts in an LLM by decoding penalty raised accuracy on hard items. No scaffold test varies the cost of losing context.
agent_test: Vary the cost of restarting an operator (context kept vs dropped) and measure dwell length.

claim: LLM overstay depends on social framing: alone, LLMs mostly divest from a failing option; under peer deliberation 99.2% escalate versus 46.2% in a hierarchy. A human-style bias against switching has not been measured in LLM agents.
agent_test: Run the Shenhav indifference-point task on the agent in single and multi-agent set-ups.

claim: The semantic-fluency finding (LLMs switch less than humans) rests on Llama-3 models and animal names only; frontier chat models and other tasks are untested.
agent_test: Replicate with a frontier model and a non-animal category.
